query: Consider the following context: The ability to endure extreme corrosion in challenging environments is reduced in stainless steel. This can be addressed by appropriate surface modification techniques to redefine the surface with the required properties. In that context, which method can be used for improved corrosion resistance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Depositing a high-entropy alloy (HEA) coating onto stainless steel using laser cladding will enhance its corrosion resistance in high-temperature molten salt environments by promoting the formation of a dense, protective oxide layer that minimizes the leaching of critical elements such as chromium.
generation.material_initial_state: Commercial stainless steel (e.g., duplex stainless steel such as DS2205) with its standard passive oxide layer, which is prone to accelerated corrosion under aggressive conditions.
generation.intervention: Apply an HEA coating (e.g., an alloy similar to AlCoCrFeNi2.1) onto the stainless steel substrate via laser cladding.
generation.conditions: Expose both coated and uncoated samples to high-temperature molten salt environments (e.g., NaCl-KCl-MgCl2) at temperatures ranging between 450°C and 650°C.
generation.structural_mediator: The laser cladding process produces a refined microstructure in the HEA coating, which upon high-temperature exposure forms a dense, self-healing oxide layer enriched in noble elements. This layer acts as a barrier to ion diffusion and minimizes galvanic effects between phases.
generation.mechanism: The HEA coating’s composition and microstructure encourage the development of a stable and compact oxide film that prevents or significantly slows the dissolution of vulnerable alloying elements (like Cr) by reducing the exposure of the base metal to aggressive molten salts.
generation.predicted_outcome: HEA-coated stainless steel is expected to exhibit a lower corrosion rate—potentially up to a fivefold reduction in mass loss—compared to uncoated stainless steel under equivalent high-temperature molten salt conditions.
generation.baseline: Uncoated stainless steel samples subjected to the same corrosion testing conditions serve as the baseline.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis may only hold in molten salt environments that allow for the stable formation of protective oxides; extreme variations in salt chemistry or thermal cycling conditions could compromise the effectiveness of the coating.
generation.uncertainty: While improvements are anticipated based on analogous results from HEA coating studies, the exact magnitude of the corrosion resistance enhancement and long-term durability under cyclic thermal and chemical stresses need further experimental substantiation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of stainless steel samples: one group with an HEA coating applied via laser cladding and one uncoated control group. Expose both groups to a molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl2 environment at 450°C and 650°C for a prolonged duration (e.g., 1000 hours). Analyze the samples pre- and post-exposure for mass loss, surface oxide development, and elemental distribution.
measurements: Surface morphology and composition analyses (using SEM, EDS)
Oxide layer thickness and integrity (using TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If after exposure the HEA-coated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in corrosion (as indicated by similar mass loss, surface degradation, and oxide layer properties compared to uncoated samples), or if the protective oxide layer is not demonstrably more stable, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs), since their discovery by Yeh et al. in 2004, [1] have opened up researchers to a new alloy system that contains five or more equimolar principal elements. In equimolar HEAs, each element has an equal probability of occupying the lattice sites in a crystal structure such as face-centered cubic (FCC), [2] body-centered cubic (BCC), [3] or hexagonal structure [4] crystal structures. Lattice distortion, sluggish diffusion, high entropy, and cocktail effects have been identified as the core effects contributing to the superior properties, hardness, strength, ductility, erosion, tribocorrosion, corrosion, and oxidation/wear resistance [5] − [7] of HEAs in a wide range of temperatures over conventional alloys. From the viewpoint of applications in extrusion dies and cutting inserts, the cost of metal powders used to develop bulk HEAs can hinder their commercialization as an alternative to the alloys in use. Abstract Dual-phase high entropy alloys have recently attracted widespread attention as advanced structural materials due to their unique microstructure, excellent mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance. However, their molten salt corrosion behavior has not been reported, which is critical in evaluating their application merit in the areas of concentrating solar power and nuclear energy. Here, the molten salt corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was evaluated in molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl 2 salt at 450 °C and 650 °C in comparison to conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205). The EHEA showed a significantly lower corrosion rate of ~1 mm/year at 450 °C compared to ~8 mm/year for DS2205. Similarly, EHEA showed a lower corrosion rate of ~9 mm/year at 650 °C compared to ~20 mm/year for DS2205. There was selective dissolution of the body-centered cubic phase in both the alloys, B2 in AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 and α-Ferrite in DS2205. This was attributed to micro-galvanic coupling between the two phases in each alloy that was measured in terms of Volta potential difference using a scanning kelvin probe.
